content: Local anaesthetic nerve blocks, such as pudendal and paracervical blocks (PCB), have been widely used for decades as a method of pain management during labour. These techniques involve the administration of local anaesthetic agents to block nerve signals and reduce pain. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of local anaesthetic nerve blocks for pain relief during labour. The review included only randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and excluded quasi-randomised studies. Data from eligible studies were extracted and analysed using standardised methods, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Out of 41 trials initially considered, 12 RCTs involving 1549 participants were included in the review. The quality of these studies was unclear, and 29 studies were excluded due to irrelevance or lack of randomisation. Comparison of local anaesthetic nerve block versus placebo or no treatment: Women who received local anaesthetic nerve blocks, particularly 2% lidocaine PCB, reported higher satisfaction with pain relief compared to those who received a placebo (one study, 198 participants; risk ratio [RR] 32.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 10.60 to 98.54). However, local anaesthetic nerve blocks were associated with a higher incidence of side effects compared to placebo (one study, 200 participants; RR 29.0, 95% CI 1.75 to 479.61). Comparison of local anaesthetic nerve block versus opioid analgesia: Local anaesthetic nerve blocks, particularly PCB, were found to be more effective for pain relief compared to opioid analgesia, such as intramuscular pethidine or fentanyl patient-controlled analgesia (one study, 109 participants; RR 2.52, 95% CI 1.65 to 3.83). The use of local anaesthetic nerve blocks was not associated with an increased rate of assisted vaginal births (two studies, 129 participants; RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.87) or caesarean sections (two studies, 129 participants; RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.87). Comparison of local anaesthetic nerve block versus non-opioid agents: Satisfaction with pain relief and the rate of caesarean sections were similar between women receiving local anaesthetic nerve blocks and those receiving non-opioid agents (one study, 100 participants; RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.84; RR 2.0, 95% CI 0.19 to 21.36, respectively). However, women who received non-opioid agents were more likely to require additional interventions for pain relief compared to those who received local anaesthetic nerve blocks (one study, 100 participants; RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.25). Comparison of different local anaesthetic agents: There were no significant differences in pain relief satisfaction, rates of assisted vaginal births, caesarean sections, maternal side effects, neonatal Apgar scores, or neonatal intensive care unit admissions when comparing different local anaesthetic agents, such as bupivacaine, carbocaine, lidocaine, and chloroprocaine. Conclusions: Local anaesthetic nerve blocks are more effective than placebo, opioid analgesia, and non-opioid analgesia for pain management during labour. However, they are associated with a higher incidence of side effects compared to placebo. Different local anaesthetic agents provide similar levels of pain relief satisfaction. The findings are based on RCTs of unclear quality and limited sample sizes. Further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these results, evaluate additional outcomes, and compare local anaesthetic nerve blocks with other pain relief modalities during labour.
